item.title: Holga Afternoon at Nau Bostik
item.description:
From 1 to 7 October, photographers all over the world take to the streets with the same plastic camera: the Holga. They do it for Holga Week, a celebration and a competition dedicated to the most imperfect and best-loved medium format camera.

We celebrate it on the 8th with an afternoon at Nau Bostik. It’s free. It isn’t a course: it’s a meet-up to shoot, share tricks and have a good time with a camera that forgives nothing and gives everything.

item.title: Learn to control light
item.description:
Where to start

Many people have been shooting for years without fully understanding why one photo comes out well exposed and another, taken in the same spot, doesn’t. The answer is always the same: light, time and sensitivity. Three variables. Nothing more.

In this workshop we work on exactly that: the relationship between aperture, shutter speed and ISO, and how to control them to get the exposure you want. We use analogue cameras because they force you to think. There’s no screen to confirm it and no app to correct it.

item.title: The first time on the street
item.description:
The street as a first time

There is an enormous difference between photographing in your own spaces —home, family, familiar places— and photographing in the street. On the street you control nothing. The light changes, people move, moments pass in a fraction of a second. And the photographer has to decide: move closer or not, shoot or not, wait or keep walking.

This workshop is for anyone who wants to make that first outing with a method. Not improvised, not left to chance: with tools for looking, for moving, and for understanding what happens when you press the shutter.

item.title: Scanning and digitisation
item.description:
The negative is the original. The scanner reads it.

A well-developed negative contains a lot of information. When you scan it badly — wrong settings, incorrect colour profile, insufficient resolution — you lose a good part of what’s on the film. And when you scan it well, you have a file that holds up for any use: a large-format print, an in-depth edit, an archive that will last for decades.

item.title: From Street to Book
item.description:
A year on the street

Street photography isn’t learnt in a workshop. It’s learnt on the street, with time, with mistakes, with a lot of looking and very little shooting. But it’s learnt much better with a framework: references to dialogue with, a group to share the process with, and someone who reads your work and asks you uncomfortable questions.

From Street to Book is a year-long course. Each month we dedicate a full session to a photographer or movement fundamental to the genre: their life, their technique, their relationship with the street. Then we go out into Barcelona and work with their gaze as the brief. Between sessions, you have assignments: a roll, a specific brief, a deliverable that the tutor reads and comments on individually.

item.title: From negative to image — digital editing for analogue photography
item.description:
Analogue photography doesn’t end in the wet darkroom. The developed negative is the raw material; digital editing is the second development. Just as in the darkroom we chose exposure time and contrast filter, in Lightroom and Photoshop we do the same — but with a precision and range of correction no enlarger can match.

This workshop is for anyone who scans their negatives and isn’t sure what to do next, or for those who already edit but want to do it with intention and stop wasting hours in front of a screen.

item.title: Photography tutorial
item.description:
A different format

Not everyone learns the same way. Some people learn better in a group; others need a space where they don’t have to follow anyone else’s pace. The tutorial is for the latter — and for the former, when they want to dig into something specific.

It might be to resolve a doubt that’s been sitting unanswered for a while. To learn to develop film for the first time without the pressure of a group. To work on a personal photographic project with someone who understands it. To review a series and find out where to improve.

item.title: Pinhole photography
item.description:
The hole that does everything

Before lenses, before optics, before 35mm cameras and everything we know as photography, there was a dark box with a small hole. Light entered, projected onto the inside and left its mark. That’s all. That is photography.

The pinhole camera isn’t a nostalgic exercise. It’s a physical demonstration of how light works. Once you’ve built it with your own hands and watched the first image appear in the developer tray, it changes the way you understand every other camera.

item.title: Cyanotype photograms
item.description:
Without a camera

Cyanotype is one of the oldest photographic techniques, invented in the 19th century. To make a cyanotype photogram you don’t need a camera, a darkroom, or any prior experience. You need paper, a chemical solution, sunlight and objects you have to hand: leaves, fabric, transparencies, anything with a shape.

You place the objects on the sensitised paper, expose to sunlight for a few minutes and rinse with cold water. Prussian blue appears. What was covered stays white; what received light turns deep blue.

item.title: Caffenol: develop with coffee
item.description:
Coffee, vitamin C and washing soda

Caffenol works thanks to the chemistry of coffee: the phenolic compounds in instant coffee act as reducing agents, converting exposed silver halides in the emulsion into visible metallic silver. Sodium carbonate raises the pH and activates the reaction; vitamin C boosts the action and helps control fog.

Unlike other alternative developers such as Guinneol or Wineol, Caffenol is surprisingly stable and predictable: the same recipe and conditions give consistent results every time.

item.title: Wineol: develop with red wine
item.description:
⚠️ Important notice: this is a highly experimental workshop

Wineol is not a stable or predictable developer. Unlike Caffenol — which gives consistent results with the same recipe — Wineol depends on many variables that are hard to control: the type of wine, its tannin content, sulphites, alcohol level, and even the batch and vintage. Two rolls developed with two “identical” wines can give radically different results. I have run experiments using exactly the same wine, temperature and chemical quantities, and the first time came out beautifully — the second time, a disaster.

item.title: Photobook: from concept to object
item.description:
An archive is not a project. A book is.

Photos on a hard drive wait. A photobook decides: which ones make it, which don’t, in what order, with what voice. Making a book forces you to understand what your images are actually about — and to defend it on every page.

This workshop is for anyone who has images and wants to make the step. It doesn’t matter whether the project is a year of street photography, a neighbourhood, a family or a darkroom process. What matters is having a real body of work and the desire to turn it into an object.

item.title: Spirit photography
item.description:
In the late 19th century, there were photographers who claimed to photograph spirits. In reality they used two things we master: exposure time and double exposure. In this workshop we teach you how they did it and put it into practice for Castanyada.

It will be on Saturday 31 October, from 7 to 10 pm, at Nau Bostik.

What we’ll do

  1. The history. 19th-century spirit photography and the fraud of the spiritualist photographers, with real examples.
  2. The technique. Long exposures with figures that move or vanish mid-exposure, and double exposures in camera.
  3. The practice. A session at Nau Bostik in low light, with torches, sheets and costumes to make our own apparitions.
  4. The developing. You can develop the film with us in a later session, if you like.

What’s included

One black-and-white film per student. If you have a camera with Bulb mode or multiple exposure, bring it; if not, we can lend you one.

item.title: Holga Afternoon: a celebration of the imperfect camera
item.description:
The Holga is a plastic medium format camera that doesn’t focus, doesn’t meter the light and forgives no mistake. And that is precisely why it is one of the best loved cameras in analogue photography.

Every year, from 1 to 7 October, photographers all over the world take to the streets with the same camera to celebrate Holga Week. We celebrate it the next day, on Thursday 8 October, with a free afternoon at Nau Bostik.

item.title: A year on the street. Twelve photographers. A book of your own.
item.description:
Street photography is not learned in a weekend workshop. It is learned on the street, with time, with mistakes and with a lot of patience. But you learn it far better if you have a frame: references to argue with, a group to share the process with, and someone who reads your work and asks you uncomfortable questions.

From Street to Book is Llumàtics’ annual course in analogue street photography. Twelve monthly sessions, each devoted to a photographer or a foundational movement of the genre. Joan Colom and Català-Roca to start at home. Cartier-Bresson, Robert Frank, Winogrand, Diane Arbus, Saul Leiter, Koudelka, Moriyama, Alex Webb and Martin Parr to widen the gaze. Every session is a different universe. Every session asks the same question: how would you do it?

item.title: Cookie policy
item.description:
What is a cookie?

A cookie is a small text file that a website stores in your browser when you visit it. Cookies allow the website to remember your preferences or actions for a period of time.

Cookies used by this website

This website is built with Hugo (static site generator). It does not use WordPress, databases or tracking scripts. Fonts are self-hosted on our server (no requests to Google Fonts).

item.title: Making a real photobook. From scratch.
item.description:
Having images is the starting point. Turning them into a book is a completely different decision. A photobook forces you to choose — which images go in, which do not, in what order, in whose voice — and every decision defines what the whole thing is about.

The new Photobook: from concept to object workshop is for those who want to take that step seriously. It is not a Photoshop course or a printing tutorial: it is complete guidance from the concept to the file ready for the printer.

item.title: Positivador WebApp, a small tool to help us in the darkroom
item.description:
In the courses we teach, students —and teachers too— have always struggled to interpret a negative image correctly. After making a direct paper negative portrait, or when looking at freshly developed film, it’s perfectly normal for our brains to have difficulty reading a negative as the image it will become once printed.

Not sure if it’s overdeveloped or underdeveloped? Still finding it hard to read shadow densities? Don’t worry! You can now download for free the Positivador web app, which we designed and developed together with LinuxBCN to make it easy to visualise the positive image directly on your phone. You can also flip it horizontally —the negative is mirrored, after all—, rotate the image, freeze the frame and —in the pro version— save it to your device.

item.title: Portrait with Holga
item.description:
The Holga and portraiture

The Holga is a plastic medium format 120 camera with a fixed 60mm f/8 lens. It has no light meter, no phase-detection focus, nothing automatic. It vignettes. The plastic lens lets light through in unpredictable ways.

And that’s precisely why it works so well for portraits.

When you photograph with a Holga you can’t rely on technique to save the image. All you control is where you place the person, how you light them and when you press the shutter. Three decisions. And in portraiture, three decisions is all you need.

item.title: Darkroom prints with your own developer — Beers Developer
item.description:
Contrast is not just a filter question

When making darkroom prints, contrast is usually controlled with multigrade filters. It works. But there is another way — older, more precise and far more satisfying: controlling contrast through the developer.

Beers Developer is a two-part formula, designed by Dr. Roland F. Beers, that produces seven different contrast grades by varying the ratio of parts A and B. Grade #1 gives the lowest contrast; grade #7, the highest. The same chemistry, completely different results.

item.title: Developing colour film as black and white
item.description:
The wrong process

C-41 colour film has its own chemistry. It needs three specific baths at controlled temperature, a precise process and a lab equipped for colour. Developing it with a black and white developer is, technically, doing it wrong.

And that’s exactly why it’s interesting.

When you develop colour film with Rodinal in stand development — a very dilute solution, no agitation, for one hour — you bypass all the logic the film was designed for. The result is neither a colour image nor a clean black and white. It’s something in between: negatives with a characteristic brown cast, very pronounced grain and a tonal range that the scanner has to push hard to read.

item.title: Guinneol: develop with Guinness
item.description:
A can of Guinness and pharmacy chemistry

Guinneol is essentially a Caffenol made with stout beer instead of coffee. The chemistry is the same: the polyphenols in Guinness act as an organic developing agent, washing soda accelerates the process, and vitamin C boosts activity and reduces fog.

It’s not a precision developer. It’s an experimentation developer — and that’s exactly why it’s worth learning.

item.title: First development: when the negative appears
item.description:
We ran the first film developing workshop. Not the first I’ve ever done, but the first here, in the new space.

The mechanics are the same as always: mix the chemicals, load the reel in total darkness, develop with care and wash with patience. But the reaction when someone opens the tank and sees the negative for the first time — that look of surprise mixed with “of course, it was always going to work” — never gets old.

item.title: Large Format Portraits — An analogue experience for everyone
item.description:
There was a moment in the workshop, while we were developing the first portrait on paper, when someone said: “Wait — you can actually see the face.” Yes. The face of the person standing in front of you, appearing in black and white inside a tray. It’s wonderful the first time. The fifth time too.

How it went

At Cameras & Films we brought our large format camera — the Woody, an old 4×5" wooden camera — and spent the morning making portraits. The setup: part of the group posed, the other part photographed, and we rotated.

item.title: Caffenol: developing with coffee
item.description:
Caffenol is one of the best-known recipes in alternative development. The name comes from caffeine + phenol, the active components that make coffee develop silver. Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) acts as an accelerator. Sodium carbonate regulates the pH. Together, a solution that genuinely works.

Why it’s worth knowing

It’s not a trick. Caffenol produces negatives you can print, scan and work with. The results have their own character: a certain softness in the grain, a tonal response slightly different from conventional developers. Not better or worse. Just different.

item.title: Cameraless cyanotype prints at Nau Bostik
item.description:
On 15 November we ran the free cameraless cyanotype workshop at Nau Bostik. Fifteen places. Fifteen people. None of them had ever made a cyanotype before.

The formula is simple: two iron salts, paper and sunlight. But “simple” doesn’t mean “no surprises”. Every sheet of paper responds differently. November light in Barcelona is not the same as August light. And the objects people bring — leaves, feathers, keys, a magnifying glass, a phone negative printed onto an acetate at the last minute — completely change the result.

item.title: World Pinhole Photography Day 2025
item.description:
On 27 April we are celebrating World Pinhole Photography Day at the Sala Basiana of the Nau Bostik.

The proposal is simple: come, experiment and take photographs with no more structure than each person wants to give it. The AWPCP.org association lends cameras to anyone who does not have one. Some of the results will be developed in the Llumàtics lab.

No plans, no rules and, above all, no lenses.

item.title: A day of analogue development: rain, Zenit cameras and a real passion for photography
item.description:
On 2 February we ran the introduction to development workshop at Cameras & Films (the former Lomography Embassy Barcelona). It was raining.

The students headed out into the streets of the Born with Zenit cameras fitted with Helios lenses and Fomapan 100. Because the light was poor, we pushed it to ISO 800. Twenty minutes on the street, then back to the lab.

From there on: loading the spiral, mixing the chemistry, developing. Ninety minutes of the complete process.

item.title: Rain, Zenits and a serious passion for analogue photography
item.description:
On 1 February, at Cameras & Films (formerly Lomography Store Barcelona), we ran one of our most beloved workshops: film developing in black and white.

Despite the day starting with a few hiccups, it ended up being a rich, rewarding experience.

The day

Rain arrived from the morning, which forced us to rethink some parts of the workshop on the fly. Light was in short supply, and I myself — yes, a little unprepared — hadn’t come ready enough for such a wet day.

item.title: Large Format Portraits at Cameras & Films — August 2024
item.description:
Bring Arezzo — said the workshop announcement — and come learn to load, focus and shoot our old large format Woody camera.

The idea: we combine the experience of operating a large format camera with portrait technique. You arrive as a photographer and leave having also been a model. Or the other way round.

Best of all: we developed the portraits immediately in the shop’s darkroom. All the magic of analogue photography, live.

item.title: Developing workshop at Cameras & Films — July 2024
item.description:
Another black-and-white developing workshop at Cameras & Films (formerly Lomography Embassy Barcelona).

Learning to develop a roll of film is one of those things that, once you’ve done it, you can’t stop. Loading the film into the tank in the dark, measuring the chemicals, checking the temperature, agitating, waiting. And when you open the tank and see there’s an image… there’s nothing quite like it.

item.title: Push processing at the Barcelona Blues Festival
item.description:
Two sessions. First the concert, then the darkroom.

Friday night we went to the Barcelona Blues Festival. 35mm rolls loaded at ISO 3200 (3-stop push). Low light, lots of grain, loads of adrenaline. Vanessa Collier on stage and us in the front row with the Leicas.

Sunday morning we came in to develop. We applied everything we’d learnt on Saturday about push development: extending the development time to compensate for the underexposure and bring back the shadows. The result: dense negatives, high contrast, expressive grain. Exactly what we were after.

item.title: Open days at the Nau Bostik
item.description:
On 26 November the Nau Bostik opened its doors. Llumàtics took part with a small exhibition of large format portraits and a simple offer: anyone who wanted one got a portrait taken.

Vintage large format camera, a Sunday morning and a lot of film.

Four session options — face or body painting, for one or two people — each with 30 minutes of analogue photographic session included. The sessions took place at the Nau Bostik.

There, surrounded by a setting and rooms that are second to none, we will go on offering training, large format sessions and a few surprises we are preparing.

At La Perversa we held an open day: the darkroom accessible, the studio available, and if you brought your camera and photographic paper, you could develop your own photos from the day. No fuss. Those who wanted to learn, learnt. Those who wanted to watch, watched.

item.title: Dr. Roland F. Beers' Paper Developer: a paper developer with contrast control
item.description:
Laboratory and more laboratory. Luckily, I love it.

I had wanted for some time to play “Breaking Bad” in the Llumàtics lab. And I had had the Formulas de Digital Truth app on my phone for a while — a good collection of chemical formulas for making developers, fixers and many other brews, experimental or not, for photography.

Thanks to Alfonso de Castro’s recommendations I focused on the Dr. Roland F. Beers’ Paper Developer. Why this one? Very simple: I could buy all the components in Barcelona and, by mixing parts A and B in different proportions, get developers with varying degrees of contrast. One developer, seven possible contrasts.

item.title: Guinneol: developing a roll with Guinness beer
item.description:
I always try out new development systems. The more experimental the better — it is the best way to keep the workshops fresh and to really understand what happens inside the tank.

This time: Guinness beer.

The recipe I found was called “Guinnes” and the translation was, let’s say, creative — it talked about “detergent” when it clearly meant soda carbonate. It is not the first time a bad translation complicates a process that should be simple. But with a bit of chemical judgement, it sorts itself out.

item.title: Analogue portrait
item.description:
The person in front of the camera

Photographing a person is different from photographing anything else. It’s not just the light, not just the technique. It’s the relationship. The way you approach, how you talk, how you make someone feel at ease in front of a lens. Without that, the best light in the world means nothing.

In this workshop we work in the Llumàtics studio: paper backgrounds, quality flash units and analogue camera. Each student takes turns as photographer and subject, and at the end we review the frames together.

item.title: B/W Film Development
item.description:
Introduction

Black and white film development is the first step towards total control of the photographic process. Unlike colour developing, B/W is robust, forgiving and gives you enormous room to experiment.

In this workshop you have learned that there is no “correct” development — there is the development that best suits your photographic intention.

History

Photographic developing as we know it today has its roots in the 19th century. Fox Talbot described in 1839 the basic principle: light-sensitive silver salts are reduced to metallic silver in the presence of a reducing agent (the developer). Since then, the chemistry has evolved but the principle has not changed.

item.title: B&W film development
item.description:
Where can I learn to develop film in Barcelona? At Llumàtics, at Nau Bostik (La Sagrera). This B&W film development workshop lasts 4 hours, includes two 35 mm rolls and all chemicals, and runs in groups of up to 4 people. Price: €220 for 1 student, €125 per person for 2, €94 for 3 and €79 for 4.

There’s no single correct development

Standard developer and manufacturer timings are a starting point, not a destination. An underexposed film needs push development to recover density. An overexposed one needs pull to avoid blown highlights. And a correctly exposed film can be developed in many different ways depending on the result you’re after.

item.title: Caffenol: alternative photographic development
item.description:
Base formula (for 500 ml)

Ingredient Quantity
Instant coffee (not decaffeinated) 14.5 g
Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃ — washing soda) 20 g
Ascorbic acid (pure vitamin C powder) 1.8 g
Distilled water to make up 500 ml

This mixture has proven effective for developing standard black-and-white film in around 15 minutes, offering a good balance of density, detail and grain.

A brief history

Caffenol emerged as a homemade alternative developer based on everyday products — primarily coffee and vitamin C — combined with sodium carbonate. It became popular in the late twentieth century among photographers looking for economical and eco-friendly developing methods that could replace traditional chemicals.

item.title: Contact
item.description:
About the workshops

How many students are there per session? +

All Llumàtics workshops have a maximum of four students per session. This small-group format allows close, personalised support adapted to each participant's pace and interests, and guarantees genuine hands-on time with the darkroom and equipment.

Do I need previous experience in analogue photography? +

It depends on the workshop. Introductory workshops (such as Photography fundamentals or Black and white developing) require no prior experience. Intermediate and advanced workshops do require completing the previous level or having equivalent knowledge. Each workshop page clearly states the prerequisites.

item.title: Cyanotype
item.description:
The blue of light

Cyanotype is one of the oldest photographic techniques: it dates from 1842. Two iron salts, paper and sunlight. That’s it. The result is a print in a deep blue — Prussian blue — that doesn’t fade, doesn’t yellow with time, and requires neither a darkroom nor hazardous chemicals.

But its simplicity doesn’t make it simple. Cyanotype responds differently to each paper, each light, each emulsion. Learning to read it is learning to respect imprecision as part of the process.

item.title: Darkroom printing
item.description:
The magical moment

There is a moment in the photographic process you never forget: when the image slowly appears in the developer tray. First a diffuse grey, then the shadows, the details, the mid-tones. The enlarger projects the negative onto the paper. Chemistry does the rest.

This workshop is the natural continuation of film development. You bring your negatives, we choose the frames worth printing and we work on the print: exposure, contrast, local controls. It’s not a complicated technique, but it requires patience, repetition and a certain feel for tone.

item.title: Development + printing in one day
item.description:
Everything in one day

The complete analogue process has two moments: film development and darkroom printing. They’re usually learned separately, in two workshops on two different dates. In this format we combine them: you develop in the morning, you print in the afternoon.

No prior experience needed. It’s a great entry point for anyone who wants to understand the full process in one go, without waiting between sessions.

How the day is structured

Morning (10:00–14:00) — Film development

item.title: DIY developers
item.description:
Understanding what you use

Most analogue photographers use commercial developers that come as powder or concentrate and follow the manufacturer’s instructions. It works. But not knowing how they’re made is like always cooking with jar sauces: efficient, but without knowing what’s inside.

In this workshop we go to the source. We study the active components of developers — developing agents, accelerators, preservatives, anti-foggants — and we prepare several formulas from scratch: the Beers Divided Developer, Caffenol and some classic and modern variants.

item.title: Experimental development
item.description:
The developer is not neutral

Standard developer and manufacturer-recommended timings give a predictable result. But predictability isn’t the only option. Temperature, dilution, time, the pattern of agitation, the chemical components — everything affects the result. And once you understand how, you can decide where you want to go.

In this workshop we explore several techniques that depart from conventional processing: push and pull, stand development (developing without agitation), Caffenol (a developer made from coffee), and the Beers Divided Developer formula — one of the most versatile artisan recipes for controlling contrast.

item.title: Introduction to Analogue Photography
item.description:
What is analogue photography?

Analogue photography — also known as film photography, traditional photography, silver-based photography or chemical photography — is the term used to describe the traditional photographic process, as distinct from the more recently developed digital photography. It is based on a physico-chemical process involving the use of photosensitive material (applied to glass plates, flexible film, or translucent material) and its stabilisation (development), in order to obtain and process images.

item.title: Introduction to darkroom printing
item.description:
The first time under the red light

Walking into a dark lab with the red light on and watching an image slowly appear in the developer tray is an experience you don’t forget. No app comes close.

This session is for anyone who has never done it. We work at the enlarger: we project the negative onto the paper, focus, expose, develop and see the result. Simple, but far more satisfying than it sounds.

item.title: Introduction to film development
item.description:
Want to learn to develop from scratch? This Introduction to film development workshop takes place at Cameras & Films (Barcelona) in collaboration with Llumàtics: we load a roll, go out shooting and develop it. 3 hours, no prior experience needed.

Everything in three hours

Analogue photography has three moments: loading the camera, photographing and developing. In this workshop we do all three, without interruption and without splitting them across different days or workshops.

item.title: Introduction to Film Development
item.description:
Materials checklist

Before developing, make sure you have everything you need:

Equipment

  • Developing tank (Patterson, Jobo or similar) + reel(s)
  • 35mm film cartridge opener: a dedicated opener, a bottle opener, or simply forcing it open
  • Accurate thermometer (±0.5 °C) — fever thermometers don’t work; they start at too high a temperature
  • Graduated measuring cylinder (500 ml or 1,000 ml)
  • Scissors
  • Funnel
  • Timer or phone
  • Opaque bottles for solutions

Chemistry

  • Developer (Rodinal, HC-110, ID-11, Caffenol…)
  • Stop bath (diluted acetic or citric acid) — we won’t be using this in the workshop
  • Fixer (Ilford Rapid Fixer, Kodak Fixer)
  • Wetting agent (Kodak Photo-Flo, Ilford Ilfotol)

Optional but useful

item.title: Introduction to large format
item.description:
Why such a big camera?

It’s a fair question. A view camera is bulky, slow, expensive to run and requires a tripod. It’s not discreet. It’s not fast. It doesn’t forgive mistakes.

And that’s precisely what makes it interesting.

When you work with large format, every exposure has a cost. Not so much financial as mental: you prepare, you meter, you check the plane of focus on the ground glass, you insert the film holder, you slide the dark slide out, and then — and only then — you expose. That deceleration demands a different quality of attention. And when the negative comes out right, you feel it.

item.title: Large format 4×5"
item.description:
One exposure, one decision

When you use a large-format camera, you don’t shoot and discard. You don’t make ten photos of the same angle to pick the best one. You make one photograph. Or two, if you’re feeling optimistic.

This completely changes how you photograph: it forces you to look for much longer, to measure the light carefully, to decide the plane of focus using camera movements no other system allows, and finally to expose a sheet — a 10×12.5 cm negative — that you develop yourself.

item.title: Large-format portrait
item.description:
A 19th-century camera

At Cameras & Films — the space that was the Lomography Embassy Barcelona, where Joan Linux has been teaching workshops since 2011 — there is a camera from the late 19th century. It’s not a museum piece. It works.

In this workshop we use this camera to make portraits. The exposure is made not onto film but directly onto photosensitive paper, which is developed immediately. The result is a unique, unrepeatable positive that condenses a hundred and fifty years of photographic history into a single session.

item.title: Learn to develop film in Barcelona
item.description:
Where can I learn to develop film in Barcelona? At Llumàtics, at Nau Bostik (Carrer Ferran Turné 1-11, La Sagrera, 08027). We run black-and-white film development workshops and C-41 development as B&W, in groups of up to 4 people.

Where to start

  • Introduction to film development — the whole process in 3 hours, at Cameras & Films, no experience needed.
  • B&W film development — 4 hours and two rolls included, to control density, push and pull.
  • Development + printing in one day — 8 hours for the whole cycle.

And then

  • Introduction to darkroom printing — your first paper prints.
  • Darkroom printing — better prints, with fibre paper.
  • C-41 development as B&W and DIY developers — to experiment.

How much it costs

Prices start at €170 (printing) and €220 (B&W development) for one student, dropping to €61–79 per person for a group of four. Materials (rolls and chemicals) are included and taxes are included.

item.title: Portrait in Large Format
item.description:
What is large format photography

Large format photography is made with specialist cameras that produce a negative (or positive) far larger than 35mm or medium format. It begins at 9×12 cm plates, continues through the classic 4×5 inches (10×12.7 cm), 13×18 cm and 20×25 cm, and extends to even larger sizes, often with custom-built cameras.

One of the primary reasons to shoot large format is the overwhelming image quality: a 4×5" negative has twenty times more emulsion area than a 35mm negative. This translates into extraordinary detail, a very rich tonal scale, and the ability to make enormous enlargements with no visible loss of quality.

item.title: Portrait in medium format 6×6
item.description:
Twelve frames to portrait a person

Portrait in medium format isn’t a technique — it’s an attitude. When you have twelve frames on a 120 roll and a waist-level Hasselblad in your hands, you don’t shoot by default. You shoot when you see it.

The square format isn’t neutral either. It centres, balances, forces you to compose differently from a rectangular frame. And the waist-level finder — camera at chest height, looking down — establishes a relationship with the subject unlike anything else. There’s nothing between you and them except the camera.

item.title: Street and gaze
item.description:
A journey, not a workshop

The difference matters. A workshop has a beginning and an end on the same day. A journey has phases: it’s prepared, executed, processed and edited. Between each phase there’s time — to let things settle, to look at the images with distance, to decide calmly.

Street and gaze is a 3 to 4-week journey through a Barcelona neighbourhood. Not the neighbourhoods you find in guidebooks. A neighbourhood with its own life, its own rhythms and people who live there — not just pass through.

item.title: Street photography
item.description:
Photographing what happens

Street photography isn’t about photographing people without them noticing. It’s not a surveillance technique. It’s a way of relating to public space: being present, looking, deciding and, sometimes, shooting.

At Llumàtics we’re interested in documentary and street photography as a form of communication — not as a technical exercise. 35mm analogue is the best tool for learning it: it limits you, makes you think, and gives you few shots to waste.

The wonderful world of Hasselblad
item.description:
A different kind of camera

The Hasselblad 500 isn’t a camera you carry everywhere. It’s a camera you use when you want to make a real photograph. The square 6×6cm format, the waist-level finder, the sound of the mirror, the interchangeable film back, the sharpness of Carl Zeiss lenses — everything invites you to slow down, look, and decide.

In this workshop there’s time for everything: to understand the system, to shoot with intention and to see the developed results the same day. We finish with a little something to eat.

item.title: Wineol: photographic development with red wine
item.description:
Wineol, base formula (for 500 ml)

Ingredient Quantity
Red wine (doesn’t need to be expensive, but must have tannins. Avoid mass-produced wines with heavy chemical treatment) 500 ml
Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃ — washing soda) 54 g
Ascorbic acid (pure vitamin C powder) 16 g
Common salt 10 g

Red wine completely replaces water: it is both the solvent and the main developing agent. The standard development time is 20 minutes at 22 °C for ISO 400 film.
